title: Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Bilateral Agreement Implementation) Bill 2014
short_title: Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Bilateral Agreement Implementation) Bill 2014

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would change the main environmental law to put a single approval process for nationally protected matters into practice.
It would make technical adjustments to existing rules for agreements between the Commonwealth and states or territories so those agreements work smoothly.

States and territories could be accredited to approve big coal and coal seam gas projects that could seriously affect water resources, but only if they promise to get and consider advice from the Independent Expert Scientific Committee.
changes: States and territories could be accredited to approve big coal and coal seam gas projects that could seriously affect water resources.
Those states or territories would have to promise to get and consider advice from the Independent Expert Scientific Committee.
The Independent Expert Scientific Committee would gain a new role: advising the Commonwealth on how a bilateral agreement is working for such projects.
People proposing projects would not need to refer matters to the Commonwealth if an approval bilateral agreement covers the action.
There would be a clear process for the Commonwealth to finish an approval if a bilateral agreement is suspended, cancelled, or stops applying to a particular action.
Minor changes would let bilateral agreements refer to the latest versions of instruments and policy documents.
summary.affected: State and territory governments, businesses proposing projects that affect nationally protected matters, and the Independent Expert Scientific Committee would be affected.

speeches.speaker: Mark Butler
speeches.brief: Opposed the EPBC Amendment (Bilateral Agreement Implementation) Bill, accusing the government of cutting about $500 million from Landcare funding and reducing a promised $600 million solar roofs commitment down to just $2 million.

speeches.speaker: Ian Goodenough
speeches.brief: Defended the EPBC bill's one-stop-shop approvals process, citing the delayed Ocean Reef Marina project in the electorate, worth an estimated $800 million, and the Neerabup Industrial Area, projected to create 20,000 direct jobs.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: Opposed the EPBC bill as putting 'the fox in charge of the hen house', warning it would hand environmental approval powers, including for World Heritage areas and threatened species like Victoria's Leadbeater's Possum, to state and even local governments, with agreements due to be finalised by September 2014.

speeches.speaker: Terri Butler
speeches.brief: Opposed handing environmental approval powers to the Queensland Newman government, citing its overturning of a 23-year ban on uranium mining, and noted the World Heritage Committee, meeting in Doha from 15 to 25 June, had expressed concern about approval for dumping three million cubic metres of dredge material near the Great Barrier Reef.

speeches.speaker: George Christensen
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, defended the Abbot Point coal port expansion as a jobs boost for Bowen and the Whitsundays after lengthy state and federal assessment delays, cited two Productivity Commission reports recommending a streamlined one-stop shop, and noted three different court cases challenging the project.

speeches.speaker: Justine Elliot
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, warning it would give state premiers including Campbell Newman, Colin Barnett and Will Hodgman control over approvals for the Great Barrier Reef, Ningaloo Reef and Tasmania's forests, and raised concerns about coal seam gas approvals on the North Coast and a proposed Kings Forest development of 4,500 lots on 880 hectares through koala habitat.

speeches.speaker: Mark Coulton
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, arguing it streamlines and in some cases strengthens environmental approvals, and accused the member for Richmond of campaigning to the 17.6 per cent of her electorate who voted Greens rather than the majority, noting she holds the lowest primary vote of any member at 33.5 per cent.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, arguing it is irresponsible to legislate while a House committee is still inquiring into environmental streamlining, said this year's budget freezes local government grants for three years at a cost of $920 million, and noted the government claims to have approved $400 billion of development investment since taking office.

speeches.speaker: Nickolas Varvaris
speeches.brief: Supported the bill as delivering a genuine one-stop shop for environmental approvals through a memorandum of understanding, updated bilateral agreements and agreements finalised within 12 months, and noted the reform was originally devised by the Gillard government in 2012 before Labor abandoned it in December 2012.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Claydon
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, warning it would hand approval powers over the Great Barrier Reef, Kakadu and Fraser Island to cash-strapped states after $80 billion in health and education cuts, cited the Places You Love alliance representing more than 1.5 million Australians across 41 groups, and highlighted the Ramsar-listed Hunter wetlands in her electorate.

speeches.speaker: Ken Wyatt
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, arguing it would speed up environmental approvals that typically take 30 to 40 days or longer, and noted that Prime Minister Gillard committed in April 2012 to finalising bilateral agreements with the states by March 2013 before the government abandoned the reform.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, listing 21 measures the Queensland government had taken against the environment, citing an Australian Institute of Marine Science finding that 50 per cent of Great Barrier Reef coral has been lost since 1960, and warned the Carmichael coal project could add up to 7,000 supertankers a year to reef shipping.

speeches.speaker: Warren Snowdon
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, citing the Northern Territory minister's approval of 400,000 tonnes of iron ore export without environmental or transport safeguards on the single-lane Roper Highway, and criticised a water licence of 21,000 megalitres granted to a Country Liberal Party donor in the Daly region, eight times more than serious farmers use.

speeches.speaker: Melissa Parke
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, citing the Supreme Court of Western Australia's ruling that state approvals for the James Price Point gas hub were unlawful, and described the south-west botanical province as one of only 34 recognised international biodiversity hotspots, home to more than 12,000 plant species.

speeches.speaker: Kelvin Thomson
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill as the worst environmental legislation the government has introduced, listing measures including 'repeal day' scrapping more than 1,000 laws and 9,500 regulations, a $484 million cut to Landcare funding, and citing analysis that 18 endemic mammal species have become extinct since European settlement.

speeches.speaker: Jill Hall
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, contrasting it with former New South Wales Premier Bob Carr's commitment to the environment, and cited a draft strategic assessment warning of serious decline in the Great Barrier Reef's coral recruitment and reef building.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill, noting it concerns the nine matters of national environmental significance set out in the act, and said the minister has offered no evidence for his assertion that state and territory governments have adequate processes for assessing environmental impacts.

speeches.speaker: Greg Hunt
speeches.brief: Defended the bill by quoting the Council of Australian Governments' communique of 13 April 2012, in which the Gillard government committed to finalising bilateral environmental assessment agreements by March 2013, argued Labor now opposes a one-stop shop process it once championed, and confirmed the water trigger will be maintained in federal legislation.

speeches.speaker: Gai Brodtmann
speeches.brief: Opposed the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Bilateral Agreement Implementation) Bill, arguing it would hand approval powers over sites like the Great Barrier Reef to state and local governments and disrespects the expertise of Commonwealth environmental scientists.
